terms.short: The pixel grid a frame is actually drawn at, before any upscaling or display scaling.
terms.definition: Render resolution is the width/height of the internal frame buffer the GPU rasterizes or ray-traces into. It can be lower than the display's native resolution (then upscaled) or match it 1:1. Lowering render resolution is the single biggest lever for GPU-bound performance because pixel-shading cost scales with pixel count.
terms.example: A 1440p monitor can render at 1080p internally and upscale to 1440p for output, trading some sharpness for GPU headroom.

terms.short: Automatically lowers render resolution under heavy GPU load to hold a target frame rate, then raises it back.
terms.definition: DRS adjusts the internal render resolution frame-to-frame (or every few frames) so the GPU can hit a target frame time even during the most demanding scenes, restoring resolution when the load drops. It trades a variable, scene-dependent sharpness for a steadier frame pacing.
terms.example: A dense particle explosion drops render resolution for a few frames so frame time stays close to target, then resolution recovers once the scene clears.

terms.short: Reconstructing a higher-resolution image from a lower-resolution render using temporal or spatial data.
terms.definition: Upscaling techniques (DLSS, FSR, XeSS, and older spatial scalers) render at a lower internal resolution and reconstruct detail using motion vectors, previous frames, or learned models, aiming to approach native-resolution quality at a fraction of the render cost.
terms.example: Rendering at 1080p and upscaling to 4K output lets a mid-range GPU sustain a target frame rate at 4K.

terms.short: NVIDIA's neural-network upscaler and frame-generation suite, exclusive to RTX GPUs.
terms.definition: DLSS uses a trained neural network running on RTX Tensor Cores to reconstruct a high-resolution frame from a lower-resolution render plus motion vectors, and (in newer versions) to generate additional interpolated frames. It requires per-game integration and an NVIDIA RTX GPU.
terms.example: A game exposes a DLSS Quality/Balanced/Performance picker that sets the internal render-resolution ratio the network reconstructs from.

terms.short: AMD's open, vendor-agnostic spatial/temporal upscaler.
terms.definition: FSR is an open-source upscaling algorithm that runs on GPUs from any vendor (not just AMD), reconstructing a higher-resolution frame from a lower-resolution render. Earlier versions were purely spatial; later versions add temporal accumulation similar to DLSS/XeSS.
terms.example: A game without an NVIDIA RTX GPU can still enable FSR to upscale from a lower render resolution on any modern GPU.

terms.short: Intel's neural upscaler, with an accelerated path on Arc GPUs and a fallback path elsewhere.
terms.definition: XeSS reconstructs a higher-resolution frame from a lower-resolution render using a trained model; on Intel Arc GPUs it runs on dedicated XMX matrix units, and on other GPUs it falls back to a DP4a compute path with reduced performance.
terms.example: The same game can run XeSS's fast XMX path on an Arc GPU and its slower DP4a fallback on a non-Intel GPU.

terms.short: Smoothing the jagged, stair-stepped edges that appear where diagonal or curved geometry meets a pixel grid.
terms.definition: Anti-aliasing reduces the visible stair-stepping ('jaggies') at polygon edges caused by rasterizing continuous geometry onto a discrete pixel grid. Techniques range from supersampling (render bigger, downscale) to multisampling (MSAA), post-process filters (FXAA), and temporal accumulation (TAA).
terms.example: Without AA, a distant power line or roofline shows a visibly stepped edge; enabling TAA smooths it using data from previous frames.

terms.short: Anti-aliasing that blends motion-compensated data from previous frames into the current one.
terms.definition: TAA accumulates sub-pixel jitter and previous-frame color samples, reprojected using motion vectors, to smooth edges and reduce shimmer over time at low extra render cost. It is the most common AA method in modern engines but can introduce ghosting or blur on fast-moving objects.
terms.example: TAA is often the default AA mode in modern engines because it is cheap relative to MSAA and pairs naturally with temporal upscalers like DLSS/FSR/XeSS.

terms.short: Anti-aliasing that samples geometry edges multiple times per pixel without re-shading the whole pixel.
terms.definition: MSAA takes multiple coverage samples per pixel at polygon edges (not full multi-sample shading), averaging them to smooth edges. It is more GPU/VRAM-intensive than TAA/FXAA and does not help with shader-based (texture) aliasing, which is why it has become less common in deferred-rendering engines.
terms.example: A 4x MSAA setting evaluates edge coverage at 4 sub-pixel positions before resolving to the final pixel color.

terms.short: A cheap post-process filter that blurs detected edges after the frame is already rendered.
terms.definition: FXAA is a single-pass post-process shader that detects high-contrast edges in the final rendered image and blurs them, at very low GPU cost. It softens jaggies but also softens fine detail and text, and does not use temporal or multi-sample data.
terms.example: FXAA is a common fallback AA option on low-end hardware where TAA's cost or MSAA's VRAM overhead is unaffordable.

terms.short: Sharpens textures viewed at oblique, shallow angles, like a road or floor stretching into the distance.
terms.definition: Anisotropic filtering improves texture sampling for surfaces viewed at a grazing angle relative to the camera, where standard mipmapping would otherwise blur the texture. Its GPU cost is low relative to its visual impact, so it is one of the few settings usually safe to max out.
terms.example: A road texture stretching to the horizon stays sharp with 16x anisotropic filtering instead of blurring into a smear.

terms.short: The resolution and mip level of surface textures loaded into VRAM.
terms.definition: Texture quality controls which mipmap level and resolution variant of each texture is loaded and kept resident in VRAM. Higher settings look sharper up close but consume proportionally more VRAM; if VRAM is exceeded, textures stream in late or get evicted, causing visible pop-in or blur rather than a frame-rate hit per se.
terms.example: Dropping texture quality one notch can eliminate texture pop-in on a GPU with limited VRAM without meaningfully changing frame rate.

terms.short: The resolution and draw distance of shadow maps, and how many cascades cover the scene.
terms.definition: Shadow quality governs shadow-map resolution, the number of cascade splits for directional (sun) shadows, and how far dynamic shadows are computed. It is one of the more GPU-expensive settings because it requires re-rendering scene depth from each light's perspective.
terms.example: Lowering shadow-map resolution one step often recovers meaningful frame time in outdoor scenes with many cascades, at the cost of softer, blockier shadow edges.

terms.short: Swapping a distant object's mesh for a simpler version to save rendering cost.
terms.definition: LOD systems substitute lower-polygon or lower-resolution-texture versions of a model as it recedes from the camera, since fine detail is imperceptible at distance. The LOD bias/distance setting controls how close an object must be before the higher-detail model is used, trading pop-in visibility against GPU/CPU cost.
terms.example: A distant crowd of NPCs renders as simplified low-poly models that swap to detailed meshes only once the camera gets close.

terms.short: How far from the camera objects and terrain continue to be rendered before they're culled or faded.
terms.definition: Draw distance sets the radius beyond which geometry, foliage, and effects are culled from rendering (or fade out) rather than drawn. Increasing it raises both CPU cost (more objects to process) and GPU cost (more pixels shaded), and is one of the more CPU-sensitive graphics settings in open-world games.
terms.example: In an open-world game, reducing draw distance for foliage and NPCs can relieve a CPU bottleneck even when the GPU has spare headroom.

terms.short: Approximates soft contact shadows where surfaces meet or crevices block ambient light.
terms.definition: Ambient occlusion darkens areas where geometry occludes ambient (indirect) light, such as corners, creases, and where objects touch the ground. Screen-space variants (SSAO, HBAO) are cheap approximations using only visible-frame depth; ray-traced AO is more physically accurate and more GPU-expensive.
terms.example: SSAO adds a soft dark contact shadow under a chair leg where it meets the floor, without a full ray-traced global-illumination pass.

terms.short: Simulating light paths (reflection, shadows, global illumination) by tracing rays instead of rasterizing approximations.
terms.definition: Real-time ray tracing casts rays from the camera or light sources to compute reflections, shadows, and indirect lighting more physically accurately than rasterized approximations, accelerated by dedicated hardware (e.g. RT cores). It is significantly more GPU-expensive than rasterized equivalents, which is why upscaling and frame generation are commonly paired with it.
terms.example: Ray-traced reflections show a correctly angled reflection of an off-screen object in a puddle, which screen-space reflection techniques cannot capture.

terms.short: A more complete, fully ray-traced lighting model that simulates the full global-illumination light path.
terms.definition: Path tracing extends ray tracing by simulating many bounces of light stochastically across a scene, converging toward physically accurate global illumination rather than approximating specific effects (shadows, reflections) separately. It is the most GPU-intensive rendering mode available in current games and typically requires upscaling and frame generation to reach playable frame rates.
terms.example: A path-traced remaster of an older game replaces its baked/rasterized lighting entirely with fully simulated light bounces, at a much higher GPU cost than the original renderer.

terms.short: Inserting AI-generated interpolated frames between rendered frames to raise displayed frame rate.
terms.definition: Frame generation (e.g. DLSS 3/4 Frame Generation) synthesizes new frames between traditionally rendered ones using motion vectors and optical flow, increasing the displayed frame rate without the GPU actually rendering that many real frames. Because the generated frames are not driven by fresh input, it raises perceived smoothness without lowering input latency the way a genuinely higher render rate would.
terms.example: A path-traced game rendering at a modest real frame rate can use frame generation to double the displayed frame rate, though input responsiveness still tracks the lower real rate.

terms.short: Synchronizes frame delivery to the display's refresh cycle to prevent screen tearing.
terms.definition: V-Sync holds a completed frame until the display's next refresh interval, preventing screen tearing (where parts of two different frames appear on screen at once) at the cost of added input latency, and can cause stutter if the frame rate can't consistently keep pace with the refresh rate. Variable-refresh-rate technology addresses the same tearing problem without the latency penalty.
terms.example: Without V-Sync, a fast-moving frame rate above the monitor's refresh rate can show a visible horizontal tear line during quick camera pans.

terms.short: The display refreshes exactly when a new frame is ready, instead of at a fixed interval.
terms.definition: VRR lets the monitor's refresh rate follow the GPU's frame output rate within a supported range, eliminating tearing and V-Sync's added latency simultaneously. It is implemented via open standards (VESA Adaptive-Sync, HDMI VRR) and vendor certification programs (G-SYNC, FreeSync).
terms.example: A frame rate that fluctuates within the monitor's VRR range displays smoothly, without the stutter or tearing a fixed-refresh panel would show at the same fluctuating rate.

terms.short: NVIDIA's variable-refresh-rate certification and (on some panels) dedicated hardware module.
terms.definition: G-SYNC is NVIDIA's VRR brand; original G-SYNC required a proprietary hardware module in the monitor, while newer 'G-SYNC Compatible' certification validates VESA Adaptive-Sync monitors work well with NVIDIA GPUs without that module.
terms.example: A monitor listed as 'G-SYNC Compatible' uses standard Adaptive-Sync hardware that NVIDIA has validated, rather than the original proprietary G-SYNC module.

terms.short: AMD's variable-refresh-rate brand, built on the open VESA Adaptive-Sync standard.
terms.definition: FreeSync is AMD's certification for VRR monitors, built on the royalty-free VESA Adaptive-Sync standard, and works with both AMD and (for many FreeSync monitors) NVIDIA GPUs since NVIDIA added Adaptive-Sync support to its drivers.
terms.example: Many FreeSync-certified monitors also work with NVIDIA's G-SYNC Compatible validation because both rely on the same underlying Adaptive-Sync standard.

terms.short: How wide an angle of the game world the camera renders, usually set in degrees.
terms.definition: FOV sets the angular width of the rendered view. A wider FOV shows more of the scene at once (useful for peripheral awareness and reducing motion sickness on large displays) at the cost of some rendering overhead and a 'fisheye' distortion at the extremes; a narrower FOV feels more zoomed-in.
terms.example: Racing sims commonly recommend calculating FOV from physical seat-to-screen distance so the in-game and real-world perceived scale roughly match.
terms.source: Field of view in video games (PC Gaming Wiki)

terms.short: The massively parallel processor that rasterizes or ray-traces frames and runs modern graphics/AI workloads.
terms.definition: A GPU is built around thousands of parallel execution units optimized for the same operation across many data elements at once (pixels, vertices, matrix math), unlike a CPU's smaller number of general-purpose cores optimized for sequential logic. Discrete GPUs have their own dedicated VRAM; integrated GPUs share system RAM with the CPU.
terms.example: A game's frame rate at a given resolution and settings is primarily determined by which GPU is installed, once the CPU and RAM are no longer the limiting factor.

terms.short: The dedicated memory on a GPU that holds textures, frame buffers, and other rendering data.
terms.definition: VRAM stores the data the GPU needs fast access to during rendering: textures, render targets, geometry buffers, and (for ray tracing) acceleration structures. If the working set of a game's settings exceeds available VRAM, textures stream in late or lower-resolution mipmaps are substituted, producing pop-in or blur rather than a clean frame-rate drop.
terms.example: Two GPUs with identical processing power but different VRAM capacity can show identical frame rates at moderate settings but diverge sharply once texture quality exceeds the smaller card's VRAM.

terms.short: The general-purpose processor that runs game logic, physics, AI, and issues draw calls to the GPU.
terms.definition: The CPU handles game logic, physics simulation, AI, asset streaming decisions, and preparing (and issuing) the draw calls the GPU then executes. In many games, especially at lower resolutions or with many on-screen entities, the CPU — not the GPU — sets the frame-rate ceiling.
terms.example: Lowering resolution alone won't raise frame rate in a scene where the CPU, not the GPU, is the bottleneck — for example a city scene with hundreds of simulated NPCs.

terms.short: A performance ceiling set by the CPU rather than the GPU — lowering graphics settings won't help.
terms.definition: A CPU bottleneck occurs when the CPU cannot prepare frames fast enough to keep the GPU fed, so the GPU sits partially idle waiting on the CPU. The signature is that lowering GPU-bound settings (resolution, shadows, ray tracing) doesn't raise frame rate, because the ceiling is set elsewhere — by draw-call count, physics load, or single-threaded game logic.
terms.example: A crowded city intersection in an open-world game may run at the same frame rate whether render resolution is 1080p or 4K, because the CPU — not the GPU — is the limiting factor there.

terms.short: A performance ceiling set by the GPU rather than the CPU — lowering graphics settings will raise frame rate.
terms.definition: A scene is GPU-bound when the GPU is the limiting factor: it is running at (or near) full utilization while the CPU has idle headroom. The signature is that lowering resolution or GPU-expensive settings (ray tracing, shadow quality, upscaling ratio) directly raises frame rate.
terms.example: A wide-open landscape with heavy ray-traced lighting is typically GPU-bound: dropping ray-tracing quality or render resolution measurably raises frame rate.

terms.short: The CPU's working memory, holding the game's loaded assets, world state, and code in flight.
terms.definition: System RAM holds the operating system, the running game process, and its loaded (but not necessarily on-screen) assets. Insufficient RAM forces the OS to page to disk, which can cause stutter during asset streaming (level loads, texture pop-in, opening menus) even when GPU and CPU processing headroom is otherwise fine.
terms.example: A game that stutters specifically when streaming in a new area, rather than during steady gameplay, often points to insufficient RAM rather than a GPU or CPU limit.

terms.short: The wait-cycle counts (CAS latency and related delays) that govern how quickly RAM responds to a request.
terms.definition: RAM timings are a set of latency values (CAS latency, RAS-to-CAS delay, RAS precharge, and others) expressed in clock cycles, which together with clock speed determine effective memory latency and bandwidth. Tighter (lower) timings at the same clock speed generally reduce memory latency, which can matter for CPU-bound scenes with heavy simulation.
terms.example: Two memory kits at the same clock speed but different CAS latency ratings will have measurably different effective latency, even though their rated speed is identical.

terms.short: A stored memory profile that lets RAM run at its rated speed/timings instead of a conservative default.
terms.definition: Motherboards default to a conservative JEDEC memory speed unless a stored profile (Intel XMP, or AMD's equivalent EXPO) is enabled in firmware, which applies the RAM's manufacturer-rated frequency, timings, and voltage. Without enabling it, RAM often runs well below its purchased rated speed.
terms.example: RAM rated for a higher frequency than the motherboard's default JEDEC speed needs its XMP or EXPO profile enabled in BIOS/UEFI to actually run at that rating.

terms.short: A CPU or GPU automatically lowers its clock speed to stay under its temperature limit.
terms.definition: When a chip approaches its maximum safe operating temperature, firmware reduces clock speed (and sometimes voltage) to bring temperature back down, protecting the hardware at the cost of performance. It shows up as frame rate or frame time that degrades progressively during a long session rather than staying stable.
terms.example: A frame rate that starts strong and steadily declines over a 20-minute session, with fan noise rising, points toward thermal throttling rather than a software issue.

terms.short: The amount of heat a cooling solution must be designed to dissipate for a given chip.
terms.definition: TDP is a manufacturer-specified figure describing the heat output a cooling solution needs to handle for the chip to sustain its rated clocks. It is a cooling-design target, not a strict power draw ceiling — actual power draw can exceed or undershoot it depending on workload and boost behavior.
terms.example: A cooler rated below a CPU's TDP is a common root cause of thermal throttling under sustained load, even if it's adequate for brief bursts.

terms.short: Lets the CPU address the GPU's full VRAM at once instead of in small windows, reducing overhead for some workloads.
terms.definition: Resizable BAR is a PCI Express feature that lets the CPU access the entirety of GPU VRAM in a single address-space window, rather than the small (typically 256 MB) windows used historically. Enabling it (in BIOS/UEFI and, sometimes, an OS/driver setting) can measurably help some games and does nothing for others, since it depends on how the game's engine streams data to VRAM.
terms.example: Whether Resizable BAR helps in a given game is workload-dependent; testing outlets typically publish per-title comparisons rather than a single universal answer.
terms.source: PCI-SIG PCI Express Resizable BAR Capability specification; AMD Smart Access Memory documentation (amd.com)

terms.short: A Windows API letting game assets stream from NVMe storage directly toward the GPU, bypassing much of the traditional CPU-mediated path.
terms.definition: DirectStorage lets compatible games load and (optionally GPU-)decompress assets from fast NVMe storage with a much smaller CPU overhead than the traditional storage stack, aimed at reducing load-time and streaming-related stutter in games with large, fast-streaming worlds.
terms.example: A DirectStorage-enabled game can stream assets from an NVMe drive with less CPU overhead than an equivalent game using the traditional Windows file I/O stack.

terms.short: How many times per second a display redraws its image, measured in hertz.
terms.definition: Refresh rate is the number of times per second a display updates its image. A frame rate above the monitor's fixed refresh rate provides no additional visible frames unless the display supports variable refresh rate; a frame rate below it can produce visible stutter as some refresh cycles repeat the previous frame.
terms.example: A 144 Hz display can show up to 144 distinct frames per second, but any frames rendered beyond that (on a fixed-refresh panel) are never displayed.

terms.short: Racing games built around physically modeled vehicle dynamics rather than arcade-style handling.
terms.definition: Sim racing titles model tire grip, suspension, aerodynamics, and drivetrain behavior with enough fidelity that real-world driving technique carries over, in contrast to arcade racers that prioritize accessible, forgiving handling. The genre is closely tied to specialized peripherals (direct-drive wheels, load-cell pedals) because standard gamepads can't convey the forces the simulation produces.
terms.example: A sim-racing title models tire slip angle and weight transfer closely enough that braking too late into a corner causes understeer the same way it would in a real car.

terms.short: Motorized resistance and vibration through a wheel that communicates road surface, grip, and load.
terms.definition: Force feedback drives a wheel's motor(s) to physically resist, vibrate, or torque the wheel in response to in-simulation forces — tire grip loss, curb strikes, road texture, aerodynamic load — giving the driver a physical channel for information a screen alone can't convey.
terms.example: A sudden lightening of steering resistance through FFB is often the earliest, most reliable warning a sim gives that the front tires are about to lose grip.

terms.short: The wheel's motor hits its output ceiling and can no longer represent forces above that point.
terms.definition: Force feedback signals are scaled to a wheel's maximum torque output; if the in-sim forces exceed that ceiling and the gain is set too high, the signal clips — the wheel outputs its maximum regardless of how much higher the true force would be, flattening useful detail (like the exact moment grip breaks) into an undifferentiated maximum.
terms.example: Setting FFB gain too high can clip out the fine detail right at the traction limit, the exact information a driver most needs to feel.

terms.short: A wheel driven directly by a high-torque motor, with no belt, gear, or pulley between motor and wheel.
terms.definition: Direct-drive wheelbases couple the steering wheel directly to a motor shaft, eliminating the mechanical play, friction, and torque limits of belt- or gear-driven bases. This gives higher peak torque and finer force-feedback resolution, at higher cost and with a correspondingly higher risk of FFB clipping if gain isn't tuned to the base.
terms.example: A direct-drive base can transmit fine road-texture detail that a lower-torque, belt-driven wheel simply cannot physically reproduce.

terms.short: The motor-and-electronics unit that drives the wheel rim; separate from the pedals and rim itself.
terms.definition: The wheel base is the motorized unit — belt, gear, or direct-drive — that a detachable steering wheel rim mounts to, and it is what actually generates force feedback. Its peak torque rating is the ceiling for how strong FFB effects can get before clipping.
terms.example: The same wheel rim can be mounted to wheel bases with very different peak torque ratings, changing how strong the FFB feels for the same in-game force.

terms.short: A brake pedal that measures the force applied, rather than how far the pedal physically travels.
terms.definition: A load cell sensor measures the pressure a driver applies to the brake pedal rather than (or in addition to) its travel distance, closely matching how real hydraulic brakes respond to pressure rather than pedal position. This allows finer, more consistent brake modulation than a travel-based potentiometer pedal.
terms.example: A load-cell brake pedal lets a driver apply the same braking pressure lap after lap even if the pedal's physical travel distance varies slightly.

terms.short: Mapping a pedal's physical input range to the game's expected 0–100% input range.
terms.definition: Calibration sets the minimum and maximum values a pedal (or wheel) reports so the game correctly maps the pedal's actual physical range to its full 0–100% input, and can apply a response curve for finer control near the pedal's most-used range. Uncalibrated pedals can leave 'dead zones' at either end or fail to reach full input at all.
terms.example: An uncalibrated brake pedal might only report 80% of its travel as usable input, meaning full physical pedal pressure never registers as 100% braking in-game.

terms.short: How many degrees the wheel physically turns lock-to-lock, matched to the car being driven in-sim.
terms.definition: Steering rotation is the total angle (in degrees) the wheel turns from full left lock to full right lock. Matching this setting to the real car's actual steering ratio — rather than an arbitrary default — is one of the most impactful, and most commonly skipped, sim-racing setup steps, since it changes how much wheel movement corresponds to a given amount of in-game steering.
terms.example: A road car with roughly 900 degrees of lock-to-lock rotation will feel unrealistically twitchy if the wheel's rotation setting is instead set to a race car's much narrower rotation range.

terms.short: The physics model that computes tire grip, slip, and force as a function of load, angle, and surface.
terms.definition: A tire model is the mathematical simulation of how a tire generates grip: how slip angle, vertical load, temperature, and surface interact to produce lateral and longitudinal force. The Pacejka 'Magic Formula' is the most widely referenced empirical tire model in both real-world vehicle dynamics and sim racing.
terms.example: A sim's tire model determines whether oversteer builds progressively and correctably, or snaps suddenly and unrecoverably, once the rear tires exceed their slip angle limit.
terms.source: Pacejka Magic Formula / tire model (Wikipedia: 'Vehicle dynamics', 'Slip angle')

terms.short: The angle between where a tire is pointed and the direction it's actually traveling.
terms.definition: Slip angle is the difference between a tire's heading and its actual direction of travel. Lateral grip force generally increases with slip angle up to a peak, beyond which it falls off — this peak-then-decline shape is what defines the difference between controlled cornering and a slide.
terms.example: A tire generates its maximum cornering force at a moderate slip angle; pushing well past that peak angle is what a slide or drift actually is.

terms.short: Recorded, time-stamped vehicle data (speed, throttle, brake pressure, tire grip, and more) captured during a lap.
terms.definition: Telemetry logs continuous vehicle and input data throughout a session, which drivers and engineers overlay and compare across laps to find where time is gained or lost — braking points, throttle application, line choice — with far more precision than watching a replay.
terms.example: Overlaying two laps' telemetry can show one driver braking a car-length later at the same corner while carrying more mid-corner speed.

terms.short: Three monitors arranged to extend peripheral field of view for a wraparound cockpit view.
terms.definition: A triple-screen setup spans three displays (typically angled) to widen the effective field of view well beyond what a single monitor can show, closely approximating a real car's peripheral vision. It requires GPU horsepower to render the combined resolution and correctly calculated per-screen FOV/bezel correction to avoid a distorted or discontinuous image.
terms.example: A triple-screen driver can see an approaching car in their peripheral vision during a lane change the way a single-monitor setup's narrower FOV would hide entirely.

terms.short: The software layer that lets the OS and games talk to the GPU's hardware.
terms.definition: A GPU driver translates API calls (DirectX, Vulkan, OpenGL) from games and the OS into instructions the GPU hardware executes, and includes per-game optimizations, bug workarounds, and shader compilation support. Driver updates can improve performance or fix bugs in specific games, but can occasionally introduce regressions — which is why driver version is a standard first question when troubleshooting new performance problems.
terms.example: A newly released game commonly ships alongside a vendor driver update specifically optimized or bug-fixed for it.

terms.short: A driver release timed and optimized around a specific game's launch.
terms.definition: Vendors (most visibly NVIDIA, with its 'Game Ready Driver' branding) release drivers timed to coincide with major game launches, containing game-specific optimizations, bug fixes, or new feature support (e.g. DLSS profile updates) for that title. These are typically more frequent, less exhaustively validated releases than a WHQL-certified driver.
terms.example: A Game Ready Driver release note might list specific optimizations or SLI/DLSS profile updates tied to a single newly launched title.

terms.short: Microsoft's certification program that a driver has passed a defined compatibility/stability test suite.
terms.definition: WHQL certification means a driver has passed Microsoft's standardized hardware compatibility and stability tests, which is generally a signal of broader validation than a rapid-cadence, game-specific driver release. Some users specifically prefer WHQL-certified drivers for stability over the newest Game Ready release.
terms.example: A user prioritizing stability over day-one game optimizations might deliberately stay on the most recent WHQL-certified driver rather than the newest Game Ready release.
terms.source: Windows Hardware Compatibility Program (Microsoft documentation, learn.microsoft.com)

terms.short: Fully removing the previous GPU driver and its leftover files before installing a new one.
terms.definition: A clean install removes not just the current driver package but its residual registry entries and configuration files (often using a dedicated uninstaller tool) before installing a new driver, to rule out conflicts or corrupted settings carried over from a previous version — a common troubleshooting step when a driver update causes new instability or performance issues.
terms.example: When a new driver introduces stutter that a previous version didn't have, a clean reinstall (rather than an in-place update) is a standard first troubleshooting step.

terms.short: Reverting to a previously installed, known-good driver version after a new one causes problems.
terms.definition: Rolling back replaces a newly installed driver with a prior version, used when a new release introduces a regression (crashes, stutter, visual artifacts) in a specific game or system configuration. It's the standard first response to a suspected driver regression, ideally paired with a clean install of the reverted version.
terms.example: If frame pacing regresses immediately after a driver update and a clean reinstall of the same version doesn't fix it, rolling back to the previous driver isolates whether the driver itself is the cause.

terms.short: Converting a game's shader code into GPU/driver-specific machine instructions before it can run.
terms.definition: Shaders are typically distributed as portable intermediate code and must be compiled into the specific GPU and driver's native instructions, either ahead of time (shipped precompiled or precompiled locally at first launch) or just-in-time as new shaders are first encountered during play. Just-in-time compilation is the direct cause of shader-compilation stutter.
terms.example: A game that pauses briefly the first time a new visual effect appears is often compiling that effect's shader on the spot rather than stalling for an unrelated reason.

terms.short: Microsoft's low-level graphics/compute API giving engines more direct control over the GPU than earlier DirectX versions.
terms.definition: DirectX 12 gives game engines more direct, lower-overhead control over GPU resource management and command submission than DirectX 11, enabling techniques like explicit multi-threaded command list generation — but it also shifts more responsibility (and more opportunity for stutter, e.g. from shader compilation) onto the engine, which previously the driver handled more transparently.
terms.example: DirectX 12 games are more likely than DirectX 11 games to show shader-compilation stutter on first encountering a new effect, because DX12 gives the engine — not the driver — more direct responsibility for that work.

terms.short: Khronos Group's open, cross-platform, low-level graphics and compute API.
terms.definition: Vulkan is an open standard, cross-vendor, cross-OS low-level graphics/compute API maintained by the Khronos Group, offering similar low-overhead, explicit GPU control to DirectX 12 but usable across Windows, Linux, and other platforms without vendor lock-in.
terms.example: A game engine targeting both Windows and Linux commonly uses Vulkan as a single low-level API rather than maintaining separate DirectX and platform-specific backends.

terms.short: How many complete frames are rendered and displayed each second, usually reported as an average.
terms.definition: FPS is the count of complete frames rendered per second. An average FPS figure can hide significant frame-to-frame variance; two configurations with identical average FPS can feel very differently smooth depending on the consistency of individual frame times, which is why frame-time and percentile-low metrics are tracked alongside the average.
terms.example: Two runs with the same average FPS can feel completely different if one has occasional long frame-time spikes that the average conceals.

terms.short: How long, in milliseconds, each individual frame took to render — the raw data average FPS is computed from.
terms.definition: Frame time is the per-frame duration, typically logged in milliseconds. Average FPS is just the reciprocal of the mean frame time, but frame time as a time series exposes variance and spikes that a single average number hides — which is why serious performance analysis works from the frame-time series, not just the FPS average.
terms.example: A frame-time graph can show a brief spike well above the average even when the reported average FPS looks perfectly smooth.

terms.short: How evenly spaced frame deliveries are in time, independent of the average frame rate.
terms.definition: Frame pacing describes the consistency of the intervals between displayed frames. Poor pacing — frames delivered in an uneven, irregular rhythm — is perceived as stutter or juddering motion even when the average frame rate is high, because motion smoothness depends on even spacing, not just frame count.
terms.example: A game can report a high average frame rate yet still feel juddery if frame pacing is uneven, because perceived smoothness tracks pacing, not the average alone.

terms.short: The average frame rate across the slowest 1% of frames in a session — a stutter-sensitive companion metric to average FPS.
terms.definition: 1% lows are computed from the slowest 1% of frame times in a measured run, converted to an FPS-equivalent figure, giving a sense of worst-case smoothness that the overall average can conceal. Testing outlets commonly report 1% lows (and the even stricter 0.1% lows) alongside average FPS specifically because a config with a high average but poor 1% lows can still feel rough to play.
terms.example: Two configurations can share the same average FPS while one has visibly worse 1% lows, meaning it stutters more often even though its typical frame rate is identical.
terms.source: Frame time percentile / '1% low' benchmarking methodology (Gamers Nexus, TechPowerUp methodology articles)

terms.short: The average frame rate across the slowest 0.1% of frames — a stricter, spike-sensitive companion to 1% lows.
terms.definition: 0.1% lows narrow the percentile-low window to the worst tenth of a percent of frames, making them more sensitive to rare but severe stutters (e.g. shader-compilation hitches) than the 1% low metric, which averages over a somewhat larger and less extreme slice of frames.
terms.example: A config with a rare but severe shader-compilation stutter might show a much worse 0.1% low than its 1% low, since the stricter metric weights that single spike more heavily.
terms.source: Frame time percentile / '0.1% low' benchmarking methodology (Gamers Nexus, TechPowerUp methodology articles)

terms.short: Brief, small, repeated interruptions in frame delivery that are individually subtle but collectively feel rough.
terms.definition: Micro-stutter refers to small, frequent irregularities in frame pacing — not a single dramatic freeze, but a persistent unevenness that degrades perceived smoothness even when average frame rate looks fine. Common causes include uneven multi-threaded frame preparation, driver overhead spikes, or background streaming.
terms.example: Micro-stutter can make a game feel subtly rough to play even when a frame-rate counter shows a stable, high average number.

terms.short: A frame-time spike caused by compiling a shader on the spot, the first time it's needed.
terms.definition: When a game compiles a shader just-in-time — usually the first time a particular visual effect or material is encountered — that compilation work can block frame delivery long enough to produce a visible, often severe, one-time stutter. Precompilation passes (a loading-screen 'optimizing shaders' step) or shader caching aim to move this cost out of gameplay.
terms.example: A new area, weapon, or effect appearing for the first time in a play session is the classic trigger for shader-compilation stutter, especially in DirectX 12/Vulkan titles.

terms.short: The delay between a physical input action and its visible effect on screen.
terms.definition: Input latency is the total time from a button/pedal/wheel action to the corresponding change appearing on the display, accumulated across input polling, game-logic processing, render queue depth, and display output. It is distinct from frame rate: a high frame rate with a deep render queue can still have noticeably high input latency.
terms.example: Technologies like NVIDIA Reflex specifically target reducing the render-queue portion of input latency, separately from raising the frame rate itself.

terms.short: The full end-to-end delay across every stage from input device to photons leaving the display.
terms.definition: System latency is the complete chain: peripheral polling, USB/wireless transmission, OS input handling, game-logic and render-queue time, GPU render time, and display processing/scan-out — every link adds to what a player experiences as responsiveness, and any one of them can dominate depending on hardware and settings.
terms.example: A wireless peripheral's polling rate, a display's processing lag, and the game's render-queue depth can each independently be the largest contributor to system latency depending on the setup.

terms.short: NVIDIA's technology for reducing render-queue-related input latency, and a companion measurement tool.
terms.definition: Reflex reduces the CPU-to-GPU render queue depth so frames are submitted closer to when the GPU actually needs them, cutting the input-latency contribution of queued frames, and separately provides in-game latency measurement overlays for compatible titles and displays.
terms.example: Enabling Reflex in a supported competitive shooter is aimed specifically at reducing input latency, independent of any change in average frame rate.

terms.short: A repeatable, controlled test run used to measure and compare performance under identical conditions.
terms.definition: A benchmark is a defined, repeatable sequence (a built-in test, a scripted replay, or a consistent manual run) used to measure frame rate, frame time, and related metrics under matched conditions, so that changing exactly one variable (a setting, a driver, a hardware component) produces a comparable, attributable result rather than noise from an uncontrolled run.
terms.example: Running the exact same benchmark sequence before and after a single settings change isolates that change's effect from the run-to-run variance an uncontrolled play session would introduce.

terms.short: An open-source tool that captures precise, per-frame timing data directly from the OS's presentation pipeline.
terms.definition: PresentMon captures frame timing at the operating system's presentation layer, giving a precise, low-overhead per-frame time series (rather than relying on in-game overlays), which is the kind of data that 1%-low, 0.1%-low, and frame-pacing analysis is computed from.
terms.example: Independent testing outlets commonly use PresentMon-based logging specifically because it captures presentation timing at the OS level rather than depending on a game's own (sometimes inaccurate) overlay counter.
